Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally strained: intense guilt, rage, and overwhelming grief on recall can co-occur, but selecting all three as core recall responses without any memory-content item suggests an over-broad affect cluster rather than a coherent memory profile.

Cross-node coherence is weak between Negative Appraisals and Memory: 'No Accountability' aligns with anger/rage, but 'Contamination' is more typical of sexual trauma or morally violating trauma and is not well supported by the rest of the assault profile.

For an adult male assaulted in a non-sexual assault profile, 'Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is clinically hard to reconcile unless other items indicate sexual assault, bodily violation, or washing/avoidance themes, which are absent here.

For an adult male assault survivor, intense guilt, overwhelming grief, and feeling dirty/contaminated can occur, but this specific combination is hard to reconcile without any accompanying sexual-assault-type cues elsewhere in the profile. The contamination appraisal in particular pulls toward a trauma meaning not supported by the other selected items.

Within the Memory node, 'Guilt on Recall' and 'Grief on Recall' are not contradictory, but paired with predominantly visual memories they imply a complex emotional recall profile that would usually be echoed in appraisals more directly tied to guilt/loss. Instead, the appraisal set emphasizes injustice, incapacity, and contamination, which do not form a tight thematic cluster.

The formulation has a strong Negative Appraisals → Threat link, so appraisals should plausibly explain the threat items. 'No Longer Capable' fits hypervigilance/feeling unsafe, but 'No Accountability' mainly reflects injustice and does not clearly drive 'Safe Zone Only' or 'Startle to Movement.' 'Contamination' especially does not map well to the selected threat items, making the appraisal-to-threat pattern clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, Self-Blame and No Accountability point in different directions of responsibility for the assault. A patient can feel both guilt and anger, but stated this strongly they suggest opposing appraisals about who is responsible.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences
issues.explanation: Memory item Guilt on Recall reinforces self-blame, which increases the inconsistency with the concurrent appraisal that perpetrators are the ones who should face consequences. The profile mixes strong perpetrator-focused blame with strong self-focused blame without a coherent bridge in the selected items.

The negative appraisal items are dominated by external blame/injustice ('the people responsible have faced no consequences', 'what happened was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it'), which fits an assault survivor, but this sits poorly with 'When I remember the event I feel intense guilt.' Intense guilt usually implies some degree of self-blame, responsibility, or perceived preventability. While mixed emotions are possible, this combination is clinically hard to reconcile here because the appraisal node contains no corresponding self-blaming belief and instead consistently locates responsibility outside the patient.

Within the Memory node, 'Guilt on Recall' is not well aligned with the other memory qualities selected ('mostly pictures or images' and 'can't put the event into words'), which describe sensory, poorly elaborated trauma memory. Those memory-form items plausibly link to threat, but guilt-on-recall points to a different meaning structure that is not supported by the selected negative appraisals. Given the formulation's strongest active pathway is Negative Appraisals → Threat, the absence of guilt-based appraisals makes the guilt memory item feel disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Kwame is a 50-year-old plumber who had built much of his identity around being the man other people called when something was broken. He had immigrated to the United States years earlier from West Africa, married, and settled into a life organized around early job calls, heavy tool bags, crawl spaces, and the steady confidence that he could handle himself. That changed after an assault several months ago. He had been finishing a late repair at a small commercial property and was loading equipment into his van when a man came up quickly from the side of the building, demanded money, and struck him when he hesitated. What stays with Kwame is not a clean story but flashes: the sudden movement at the edge of his vision, the man’s arm lifting, the glint of metal from a tool lying near his own open van, the pavement rushing up, and the feeling that in the crucial second he did nothing right. When he tries to describe it, his words thin out. He says he can “see it all” but cannot tell it straight through, and each return of those images brings a crushing sense that he failed some basic test of judgment and strength.

In the first weeks afterward, Kwame found himself replaying those pictures without warning. He did not think of them as memories arriving in an orderly way; they were more like abrupt visual intrusions that took over his attention. A figure stepping out from behind shelving at the hardware store, a customer appearing beside him while he worked under a sink, even his wife moving suddenly in the kitchen could pull his body into the same jolt of danger before he had time to think. At night he lay awake braced for something he could not name, and when he did sleep it was shallow and easily broken. The more these picture-like fragments returned, the more certain he became that danger was close and that his body had to stay ready.

As the months passed, the meaning Kwame made of the assault hardened. He had come to believe that what happened was profoundly unfair and that no one had answered for it, and that belief kept the event feeling unfinished rather than over. Even more painful was the conclusion he drew about himself. Before, he had thought of himself as capable, decisive, the person who knew what to do in tight spaces and difficult situations. Now he was certain he could not trust himself to respond correctly if something happened again. That loss of confidence narrowed his world. He only felt truly safe in a very limited set of places—his bedroom with the door locked, a particular chair in his living room, his own truck when parked in his driveway—and outside those places he scanned constantly. On jobs, if someone moved unexpectedly in a hallway or came up behind him while he was checking pipes, he would jerk, turn sharply, and feel ashamed immediately afterward. In his mind, the problem was not only that the world had become dangerous, but that he was no longer the man who could manage it.

That sense of threat fed back into the way the assault lived in his mind. Because he spent so much of each day on edge, sleeping lightly and startling at sudden movement, the event never settled into the past. Instead, it kept returning in fragments, vivid and sensory, especially when he was tired. He might be crouched under a sink in a client’s bathroom, hear footsteps entering the room, and in an instant be back inside the same visual burst of the attack, unable to put any of it into words except to say, “I see it.” The guilt arrived with the images: he should have noticed sooner, moved faster, protected himself better. His wife has seen him sit silent after one of these episodes, staring ahead, unable to explain what just passed through him.

The assault has altered his work and his marriage in concrete ways. He now avoids late service calls whenever he can and refuses jobs in isolated buildings, which has begun to affect his income and has led to tension with a contractor who used to rely on him. Even routine appointments are difficult because plumbing work places him exactly where he feels most exposed—bent over, focused on a task, with people entering and leaving around him. At home, he keeps to his few safe places and checks locks repeatedly before bed. The nights are the worst; once awake, he listens for movement and cannot relax enough to return to sleep.

Kwame finally sought help after startling so violently when a customer came around a corner at a job that he dropped a wrench and cut his hand. What frightened him most was not the injury but the thought, immediate and familiar, that he could no longer trust himself to do the right thing in a critical moment. He says he wants to sleep, to work without feeling hunted, and to be able to tell what happened without being overtaken by the pictures and the guilt. At the same time, he is afraid that the assault revealed something permanent—that his world is no longer safe except in a few shrinking places, and that the capable man he was before may not return.
